cards.title: Don't Do This If You Like This hook
cards.summary: Curiosity-plus-relatability hook format that opens short-form video with a forbidden-action premise tied to the viewer's existing desire.
cards.use_when: Writing the opening 1-3 seconds of a TikTok/Reels creative for a consumable or habit product (appetite suppressant, snack, supplement, beauty routine) where you need to stop the scroll before pitching.
steps: Frame the hook as a restriction on something the target buyer already loves: 'don't drink this if you like eating' — the audience's love of food creates the relatability, the restriction creates the curiosity gap.
Cast a creator who visibly embodies the tension (e.g. someone who describes themselves as 'a foodie') so the premise reads as personal experience rather than a scripted claim.
Deliver the payoff through first-person storytelling ('if I don't eat before I drink this I'll forget to') rather than a feature list; the product is the implied resolution, not the opening subject.
Treat this as a three-purpose asset: post organically, hand to affiliates, and run as a paid ad — the same file can serve all three.
Match price to impulse range for TikTok: the source cites examples around $29-$39 as a range that still leaves margin.
caveats: Source is one practitioner's breakdown of TikTok Shop examples; cited view/sales figures are individual case results, not benchmarks.
The 'don't do this' construction can read as fear-baiting if the restriction is not genuinely connected to the audience's desire.

cards.title: Problem/Solution comparison video with competitor callouts
cards.summary: Side-by-side demo that names specific competitor failures and demonstrates your product solving them in one continuous shot.
cards.use_when: Producing creative for a product in a category crowded with lookalike competitors (phone accessories, cleaning tools, kitchen gadgets) where buyers need a logical reason to switch.
steps: Open by calling out the problem in the viewer's own words ('if you see a lot of dust...'), then immediately show two competing products failing — they break, scratch, or misalign.
Demonstrate your product doing the exact tasks the competitors failed at, on camera and in one take, so the comparison is visible rather than asserted.
List multiple competitor reasons-to-leave and multiple of your benefit-reasons-to-buy so the difference is unambiguous.
Use conditional logic scripts to move the viewer toward self-identification: 'if you're experiencing X problem you need this; if you're using X product and not seeing X result you should use this.'
Build the demo as its own setting (a tabletop, a bathroom counter) rather than cutting between clips — the source argues better demonstration correlates with more sales than raw view volume.
Note the source's example: high views (tens of millions) did not automatically produce proportionally high sales — demonstration quality mattered more.
caveats: Calling out named competitors may expose you to platform ad policies and comparative-advertising rules; verify current TikTok ad policy before running as paid.
The source's 'over-exaggerated' problem visuals (implausibly dirty phone) are his example — overstating a problem can damage trust if the audience finds it implausible.

cards.title: Transformation teaser: tease the result, don't reveal it
cards.summary: Curiosity-driven creative that withholds the end result and only hints at the transformation, using sound overlay and ingredient highlights.
cards.use_when: Creating branded creative for a results-based product (fitness drink, protein, skincare, body transformation) when you have no influencer and need a low-production asset for your own page.
steps: Write an on-screen or voiceover tease of the future state without showing it — the source's example is a countdown-to-vacation beach/bikini/abs line over a product shot.
Highlight 2-3 key ingredients or specs visually (protein content, active compound) so the product reasons are present even though the outcome is hidden.
Keep it short — the source's example is only a few seconds long — which makes it cheap to produce repeatedly at volume.
Apply the same format to before/after content: show before and after, or show only the before with a telegraphed after.
Publish it as branded creative on your own page; the source notes this format does not require an influencer or affiliate.
caveats: The source asserts curiosity/controversy/mystery consistently outperforms straight product showcases — treat as his opinion, not a measured rule.
Teasing a transformation invites skepticism; comment-reply videos are the follow-up mechanism he recommends for handling doubt.
Cited view and sales figures (e.g. 203k views, ~$5k sales) are a single case example, not a forecast.

cards.title: Reaction-style video: bottle the response on camera
cards.summary: Capture a real physical or emotional reaction to the product in one take and let that reaction carry the ad.
cards.use_when: Producing creative for products with a sensory or dramatic payoff — supplements, flavors, taste tests, nasal sticks, clothing transformations, before/afters.
steps: Identify whether your product produces a sensation or visual change 'a magnitude higher than normal' — the source says the format works only where the reaction is genuinely strong.
Set a one-take scenario: street interviews, gym taste tests, or a person trying the product for the first time; the source's example opens with 'two, one, take a deep breath' before the reaction.

Capture the unfiltered physical or facial response rather than describing the product; the viewer's curiosity about what they don't yet know (what it smells like, feels like) drives questions and sales.
Use the reaction as the hook and place product explanation and CTA after it, keeping the back end explicit.
Expect this format to also build the account itself — the source credits this strategy alone for driving follower and view growth.
Extend the format to a 'what you wear now vs. what you should be wearing' comparison for apparel, capturing the person's reaction to the change.
caveats: The source's agency client growth claim is a self-reported case example, not a guaranteed outcome.
Reaction content can feel staged; using real first-time participants is what makes it land.

cards.title: Misconception video: use a credible source to reframe a belief
cards.summary: Break down a common consumer myth with an authoritative voice, then position your product as the corrective action.
cards.use_when: Writing creative for a category with entrenched wrong beliefs or low awareness of the mechanism (sleep, breathing, skincare, nutrition) where you need to create demand for a solution buyers don't know exists.
steps: Open by naming the belief the audience holds ('mouth breathing during sleep is harmless') and then contradict it with a specific, credentialed source or study reference shown or spoken in the video.
Spell out the consequence the audience didn't know: the source cites a Stanford study example contrasting mouth-breathing and nose-breathing twins and claimed facial-structure differences.
Only after establishing the misconception, introduce your product as the fix — a sleep mouth tape being worn during sleep to change the outcome.
Anticipate pushback: the source says this format generates questions in the comments, which is an asset — reply with comment-reply videos and link to the product from there.
Reuse the format for 'if you always believed you should do X, you're actually wrong' framings aimed at viewers who currently choose a competing behavior.
caveats: Claims of scientific consensus must actually be accurate; using a credible source is the mechanism, and misattributing studies will backfire in comments.
The source's example generated comparatively modest sales (~3,400) despite decent views — this format builds audience and questions more than immediate volume.
The presenter's use of an attributed study is summarized here as his example; verify any specific study before citing it in your own creative.

cards.title: Comment-reply video: turn audience questions into creative
cards.summary: Film a direct reply to a high-engagement comment, demonstrating the product while answering the viewer's skepticism.
cards.use_when: Finding your next winning creative angle, or answering the objection that keeps appearing in your TikTok/ad comments (does it actually work, how does it stay on).
steps: Scan comments for a question or disbelief statement with visible likes and replies — that is the demand signal, and replying to it re-serves the video to everyone who engaged with that comment.
Open the video visibly replying to the comment, then demonstrate how the product works in a visual, sensory way rather than explaining it abstractly ('they grip to your body heat, not sticky').
Show the before/after or the mechanism directly so the skeptic sees it resolved on camera.
Link directly to the product from the video and reuse the asset as a paid TikTok ad to scale it beyond organic reach.
Accept that some comment replies go viral for the wrong reasons — the source argues the algorithm generally routes it to the right audience anyway.
caveats: The social-proof lift from replying to a liked comment is the source's stated mechanism; treat as his observation.
A video that goes viral for unintended reasons can still spend budget inefficiently — monitor who is actually converting, not just view volume.

cards.title: Free tip / secret narrative that resolves into a product pitch
cards.summary: Tell a personal tip or 'secret strategy' story that feels like raw testimony, then reveal the product as the mechanism behind it.
cards.use_when: Writing creative for a supplement or consumable where buyers already live with a specific recurring annoyance (nighttime bathroom trips, poor sleep) and will watch a peer's story.
steps: Lead with the problem state in the viewer's voice — the source's example is waking multiple times a night to use the bathroom.
Frame the answer as a tip or secret you were reluctant to share ('I actually just listened to my wife, she was spot on') so the opening reads as storytelling, not advertising.
Reveal the tip is actually a product — the source's example is two products, one positioned as a nitric oxide/blood flow booster.
Keep the video looking like raw, natural storytelling rather than a polished ad, and place the pitch in the middle-to-back half.
Hook at the start, explain the product in the middle, and close with a clear call to action.
Use the format as a template across organic, affiliate, and paid placements from one shoot.
caveats: Health-adjacent claims (blood pressure, circulation) require compliance review before use as a paid ad — verify current platform and regulatory rules.
The source's ~1.3M views and ~$22k sales are a single example, not a performance expectation.

cards.title: Hook-Value-CTA structure for short-form direct response
cards.summary: The repeatable back-end structure the source applies across all reviewed formats: hook immediately, deliver value in the middle, pitch product and CTA at the end.
cards.use_when: Structuring any TikTok/Reels creative for a product, especially when adapting an existing winning format to a new product or angle.
steps: Choose one hook format for the opening seconds — a reaction, a free tip, a 'don't do this' restriction, a misconception, or a problem callout.
Deliver the middle as relatability or value: raw storytelling, demonstration, or breakdown of the problem, with the creator explaining the product inside that story rather than as a standalone pitch.
Place the product reveal and call to action in the middle to back end, so the viewer is already engaged before the ask.
Keep the whole thing looking non-ad-like: the source emphasizes every reviewed video is positioned to feel relatable and native rather than produced.
Ship each asset simultaneously to three channels — organic post, affiliate content, and paid ad — so one production serves reach, affiliate sales, and scaled spend.
caveats: The hook framing is the source's opinion on what drives view volume; test hooks against your own audience rather than assuming one dominates.
The 'use one video in all three channels' workflow depends on affiliate program terms and ad rights — confirm permissions before repurposing creator content as paid.

cards.title: Bundle strategy to raise AOV when unit price is too low
cards.summary: Answer to low-margin unit pricing by selling multipacks rather than trying to raise the single-unit price.
cards.use_when: Pricing or merchandising a low-ticket product (the source's example is ~$4.99) where a single unit cannot carry ad spend, or when planning bundles for a consumable.
steps: Diagnose whether the single-unit price can support paid acquisition — if not, don't simply raise the unit price; consider stackable multipacks instead.
Create 3-pack, 5-pack, and 6-pack options that lift AOV to roughly $25-$30 in the source's example.
Present the bundle as the default purchase path so the buyer's decision is pack size, not whether to buy.
Check that the bundle makes sense for a consumable replenishment cycle so repeat purchase and AOV move together.
Combine with a video format that already sells on curiosity (misconception, free tip, reaction) so the creative drives to a higher-value offer.
caveats: The specific $4.99 -> $25-$30 figures are the source's example of what other sellers were doing, not a validated benchmark for your product.
Multipack pricing must still show a credible per-unit saving versus single units or buyers will comparison-shop against it.

cards.title: Match creative format to product type
cards.summary: Selection guide mapping the source's seven video formats to the product characteristics that make each one work.
cards.use_when: Planning a creative testing slate for a new product launch or deciding which format to shoot first when budget or shoot time is limited.
steps: If the product produces a strong sensory or emotional response on first use, start with reaction-style — the reaction itself is the hook.
If buyers currently use a flawed competitor product, start with problem/solution competitor comparison so the switching logic is visible.
If the product has an aspirational outcome that takes time (fitness, body, skin), use a transformation teaser rather than a product showcase.
If the category is full of false beliefs, use a misconception video with a credible source to create demand, then position the product as the fix.
If the product is a consumable tied to a recurring annoyance, use the free-tip/secret narrative; if it looks visually surprising in use, use comment-reply demonstration.
If the product has a strong desire-based restriction (eating, drinking), use the 'don't do this if you like this' hook.
Shoot each selected format with the hook-value-CTA structure and distribute to organic, affiliate, and paid.
caveats: These pairings are the source's practitioner heuristics from TikTok Shop examples, not tested universal rules — validate with your own creative testing.
A single product can support multiple formats; treat this as a starting slate for testing, not a permanent assignment.
